title: Weekly Essay Writing Schedule by CEFR Level | Hacé Cuentas
h1: Weekly Writing Practice by Language Level
description: Plan weekly writing volume by CEFR level (A1 100 words/week up to C2 2,500+). Research-backed schedules for TOEFL, IELTS, DELE, DELF prep. Free calculator.
intro: If you're learning a second language and your speaking has plateaued, the missing piece is almost always written output. As a language coach, I tell every student the same thing: writing closes the productive-receptive gap faster than any other activity, because it forces you to retrieve, organize, and commit to the grammar and vocabulary you've been passively absorbing. This calculator gives you a weekly word-count target mapped to your current CEFR level so you stop guessing how much is enough. The research-backed baselines are: A1 around 100 words per week (very short, high-frequency vocabulary), A2 200 to 300 words, B1 around 500 words, B2 800 to 1,000 words, C1 1,500+ words, and C2 2,500+ words for advanced maintenance or exam prep. These numbers align with Krashen's i+1 comprehensible input principle applied to output (Swain's output hypothesis), and with Lichtman and VanPatten's 2021 review showing that explicit writing instruction combined with structured practice schedules produces measurable gains in accuracy and fluency at every level. Whether you journal informally or grind structured essays for the TOEFL or DELE, the volume targets below are what actually move the needle.
keyTakeaway: **Weekly Word Output = Sessions per Week × Words per Session.** Hit your CEFR-level target consistently for 8–12 weeks before expecting visible gains. Volume beats perfection at every level below C1.
useCases: A B2 English learner preparing for the TOEFL iBT or IELTS Academic exam who needs 800–1,000 words per week split across timed Task 1 and Task 2 essays to hit Band 7+ in 12 weeks.
A B1 Spanish learner prepping for the DELE B1 exam — needs 500 words per week across short narrative and informal letter tasks to consolidate preterite vs imperfect distinction before test day.
A C1 French learner studying for DELF C1 — daily 45-minute structured essay sessions (1,500+ words/week) on argumentative topics with delayed self-correction to refine subjunctive and connector use.
An adult hobby learner at A2 level who wants a sustainable 200 words/week schedule (two short journal entries) to build the habit without burnout before scaling up.
A polyglot at C2 in three languages running a rotating maintenance schedule: 2,500 words/week in the strongest language, 1,500 in the second, 800 in the third, switching emphasis monthly.
explanation:
## CEFR Writing Descriptors — What Each Level Actually Means

The Council of Europe's CEFR Companion Volume (2020 update) defines written production at every level. These descriptors drive everything in this calculator:

- **A1** — fill in forms with personal details, write simple isolated phrases and sentences (name, address, where you live).
- **A2** — write short, simple notes and messages relating to immediate needs (postcards, simple personal letters about daily life).
- **B1** — write straightforward, connected text on familiar topics, linking shorter discrete elements into a sequence (informal letters, blog entries describing experiences).
- **B2** — write clear, detailed text on a wide range of subjects, evaluating ideas and giving reasons for opinions (TOEFL Independent essay, IELTS Task 2 discursive essay).
- **C1** — write clear, well-structured text on complex topics, underlining relevant salient issues, expanding and supporting points with subsidiary points (academic essays, professional reports, opinion editorials).
- **C2** — write coherent, complex texts with logical structure that helps the reader find significant points (publication-quality articles, academic theses, sophisticated argumentation with hedging and concession).

## Spaced Output Schedules That Actually Work

Writing once a week for two hours is the worst possible schedule. Distributed practice — multiple short sessions across the week — beats massed practice for retention by roughly 200% (Cepeda et al., 2006). Here are coach-tested schedules by level:

- **A1**: 3x per week, 15 minutes per session, ~35 words each → ~100 words/week. Focus on Subject-Verb-Object with high-frequency vocabulary.
- **A2**: 3–4x per week, 20 minutes, ~75 words each → ~250 words/week. Short personal narratives, simple connectors (and, but, because).
- **B1**: 4x per week, 25–30 minutes, ~125 words each → ~500 words/week. Connected paragraphs, past tenses, opinion with reasons.
- **B2**: 5x per week, 30 minutes, ~180 words each → ~900 words/week. Argumentative structure, range of cohesive devices. Add timed exam essays (40 min for IELTS Task 2) once weekly.
- **C1**: Daily, 45–60 minutes, ~250 words each → ~1,750 words/week. If you're prepping for Cambridge CAE/CPE, TOEFL above 110, or IELTS Band 8+, daily is non-negotiable.
- **C2**: Daily, 60+ minutes, 350–400 words each → 2,500+ words/week. Maintenance for proficient speakers; rotate languages if multilingual.

## Error-Correction Modalities — The Truscott Debate

John Truscott's 1996 paper *The Case Against Grammar Correction in L2 Writing Classes* set off a 30-year argument that still isn't settled. The 2010 Truscott vs Bitchko follow-up confirmed the practical consensus most coaches operate on:

- **Delayed self-edit beats real-time correction.** Write the full draft uninterrupted. Wait 24 hours. Re-read and correct your own work before getting external feedback. The 24-hour gap is when consolidation happens.
- **Selective correction beats comprehensive correction.** Focus on one error category per week (e.g., only verb tenses, then only articles, then only prepositions). Highlighting every error overwhelms working memory and produces no retention.
- **Human native correctors > AI for nuance.** [LangCorrect](https://langcorrect.com) is the current go-to free community where natives correct your text in exchange for you correcting theirs. [italki](https://italki.com) offers paid essay-correction packages at $5–15 per essay from professional tutors. Lang-8 was the legacy platform — mostly defunct now.
- **AI feedback (Grammarly, DeepL Write, ChatGPT) is great for first-pass mechanical errors but poor for register, idiom, and pragmatic appropriateness.** Use AI tools to catch typos and basic agreement, then send the cleaned-up draft to a human for the stuff that matters.

A strong ChatGPT prompt for essay feedback: *"You are a CEFR-certified [target language] examiner. Review this [B2/C1] essay for grammar, lexical range, cohesion, and task achievement. Score 0–9 per CEFR descriptor and give three specific improvements."*

## Genre Rotation by Level

Writing the same kind of text over and over produces a narrow skill. Rotate genres as you climb:

- **A1–A2**: descriptive — describe your room, your routine, your family. Builds noun phrases and present tense.
- **B1**: narrative — past-tense storytelling, personal experiences, blog-style entries. Drills past-tense system.
- **B2+**: argumentative — opinion essays with thesis, body paragraphs, counter-argument, conclusion. Builds the discursive structure tested in TOEFL, IELTS, DELE, DELF.
- **C1+**: academic — essays with citations, reports, literature reviews. Hedging language (it could be argued that, this suggests), nominalisation, formal register.

## Tools Worth Your Time

- **LangCorrect** (free) — community native correctors, daily writing streaks, multiple target languages.
- **italki** ($5–15/essay) — paid tutor essay-correction services for serious exam prep.
- **Grammarly + DeepL Write** — first-pass mechanical correction, especially useful at B2+ when you can recognize most errors yourself.
- **A simple paper notebook** — still the most undervalued tool, especially at A1–A2 where typing speed exceeds processing speed and produces sloppy output.

## Common Mistakes I See in Coaching

1. **Writing without a prompt.** Free-form journaling at B1+ defaults to comfortable vocabulary. Always use a prompt to force productive struggle.
2. **Skipping the 24-hour gap.** Correcting your essay the moment you finish writing it bypasses the consolidation window. Sleep on it.
3. **Quantity without feedback.** 1,000 words a week with zero correction reinforces fossilized errors. At minimum, run it through an AI tool.
4. **Ignoring exam timing.** From B2 onward, at least one weekly essay should be timed to exam conditions (40 min for IELTS Task 2, 30 min for TOEFL Independent).
5. **Stopping at the word count target.** The target is the floor, not the ceiling. If you're hitting 1,000 words at B2 comfortably, you're ready to scale up.

faq.q: How long should I write daily to reach B2 in 6 months?
faq.a: Realistically, moving from B1 to B2 in 6 months requires roughly 200–300 hours of focused study, of which writing should be 25–30% (50–90 hours total). That works out to 30 minutes of writing 5x per week, hitting ~900 words/week. Combine with daily reading at i+1 difficulty and 2x weekly tutor sessions. Sub-200 hours and you're unlikely to consolidate the B2 written production descriptors (extended argumentation, range of cohesive devices).

faq.q: Should I self-correct or get native correctors?
faq.a: Both, in this order: write the draft, wait 24 hours, self-correct what you can spot (this is where most learning happens), then send to a native via LangCorrect or italki for the stuff you can't see. Truscott's 30-year debate landed here: selective, delayed correction with learner involvement beats comprehensive real-time correction every time. Skipping the self-edit step and going straight to a corrector is wasting the consolidation window.

faq.q: Is ChatGPT or Grammarly feedback good enough for essay correction?
faq.a: Good enough for first-pass mechanical errors at any level — typos, basic subject-verb agreement, article use. Not good enough for register (formal vs informal), idiomatic appropriateness, or task achievement at B2+. My recommendation: run the draft through Grammarly or DeepL Write to catch the obvious stuff, then send the cleaned version to a human via LangCorrect (free) or italki ($5–15) for nuance. Using AI alone past B2 leaves a ceiling on your output quality.

faq.q: How do I self-assess my writing CEFR level accurately?
faq.a: Three checkpoints: (1) Read the Council of Europe CEFR Companion Volume written production descriptors and honestly identify the highest band where you can produce all the criteria — not just some. (2) Take a free official sample test (Cambridge English, DELE Instituto Cervantes, DELF France Education International all publish free sample writing tasks). (3) Submit a 250-word essay to LangCorrect or italki for level assessment. Self-assessment alone tends to overshoot by half a level; combine all three.

faq.q: Is handwriting better than typing for language practice?
faq.a: At A1–A2, handwriting wins. Typing speed exceeds processing speed at beginner levels, which produces sloppy output and bypasses the slow retrieval that consolidates vocabulary. From B1 onward, typing is fine — and necessary if you're prepping for TOEFL iBT (typed) or any computer-based exam. For DELE, DELF, and Cambridge handwritten exams, do at least 30% of your weekly volume by hand to build wrist stamina.

faq.q: Can I write about the same topic every day?
faq.a: No. Same topic = same vocabulary recycled. The point of writing practice is to force retrieval of vocabulary and grammar you'd otherwise lose. Rotate prompts daily across genres (description Monday, narrative Tuesday, opinion Wednesday, etc.) to keep stretching the productive range. The exception is exam prep in the final 2 weeks before test day, when you should drill the exact prompt format you'll see on the test.

faq.q: Should I write short stories or argumentative essays?
faq.a: Depends on level and goal. At B1, narrative short stories drill the past tense system, which is the B1 grammatical bottleneck — do those. At B2+, argumentative essays are what every major exam (TOEFL, IELTS, DELE, DELF) tests, so prioritize those if you have an exam date. For general fluency at C1+, alternate weekly: argumentative one week, narrative the next, descriptive the third. Variety beats repetition past B2.

faq.q: What if I miss a few days — does my schedule reset?
faq.a: No reset, just resume. The 8–12 week consolidation window assumes ~75% adherence, not perfection. Missing 2–3 days a month is normal and won't derail progress. What does derail you: missing 2+ weeks in a row, which lets the productive vocabulary network start to atrophy. If you have a long gap, drop one CEFR sub-level (e.g., B2 down to B1+) for the first week back to ease in, then return to target.
